title: The sultan came to her: Tétouan's woman governor was no pirate
dek: Sayyida al-Hurra governed Tétouan for more than twenty years, built shipyards and worked with Ottoman privateers against Spain and Portugal; European sources call her a pirate, while recent scholarship treats her as an example of early decolonial practice.
why: The middle stretch untangles pirate from privateer, and shows how the standpoint of the surviving sources shapes the history — a payoff beyond the biography. The listener mail at the end is skippable.
who: Content writers working on North African and Mediterranean trade, or interested in case studies of women governing; if you are short on time, listen only to the middle section on privateering and skip the mail at the end.
skip: The listener mail at the end (Shakespeare's birthplace and canvas shoes) can be skipped in full; the main piece ends before 28:47.

points.h: Her title meant noble, powerful, independent — not pirate
points.body: The episode opens with its most important judgment: European sources compress Sayyida al-Hurra's whole life into the word "pirate," but the label cannot account for the full picture. Sayyida al-Hurra is an honorific, literally carrying senses like "noble, powerful, independent," and it was used for other Muslim women as well, among them the twelfth-century Yemeni ruler Arwa al-Sulaihi. She was probably born somewhere between 1485 and 1495; her father was Ali ibn Rashid, a prince of sharifian descent, and she grew up in the multiethnic community of Chefchaouen, fluent in Arabic, Spanish and Portuguese.

points.h: The city she governed was a fortification and a refugee camp at once
points.body: Chefchaouen was built in the Rif mountains, roughly 60 kilometers from the coast, precisely to defend against Portuguese incursion after Portugal took Ceuta in 1415. In the same era, Spain conquered Granada in 1492, ending the Reconquista, and issued the Alhambra Decree that same year expelling Jews; Muslims were then required to convert or leave in 1502 and 1526. Chefchaouen and Tétouan consequently filled with Muslims, Jews and converted Muslims (Moriscos) fleeing the Iberian Peninsula, forming refugee communities that were diverse but not entirely equal.

points.h: Her governorship came from her brother's appointment, not from inheritance
points.body: In 1510 she married Mulay al-Mandri, the governor of Tétouan — a political marriage joining two families and two parts of the region, Chefchaouen and Tétouan. Because she was educated, she was able to assist her husband in governing from the start, and when he traveled her share of the rule was gradually formalized. Her husband died around 1519 and his brother wanted to seize power, but her own brother Ibrahim, serving as vizier in Fez, named her the successor. It was not common for a woman to hold that kind of power, yet she appears to have won the trust of the population and was accepted as governor.

points.h: Her ships guarded the coast and also captured Spanish and Portuguese vessels
points.body: Facing continuous pressure from Portugal and Spain, and a Moroccan economy in decline as European shipping routed around Africa, she worked with the Ottoman privateers Oruç Reis and Hızır Reis (often lumped together as "the Barbarossa brothers"). The two were sons of a potter from Lesbos, first served a sultan's son, later were hired by Algiers, and ultimately served the Ottoman Empire. She built shipyards where the Ottomans could construct and berth ships, and she also expanded her late husband's fleet; those ships both defended Morocco and attacked and captured Spanish and Portuguese ships, with captives held at Tétouan awaiting ransom.

points.h: If holding captives for ransom counts, Elizabeth I was a pirate too
points.body: Holding captives and demanding ransom from their home country cannot on its own be the line that makes her a pirate, because the practice was fairly common at the time. The episode notes that Oruç was once captured by a knightly order and freed when his brother Hızır paid the ransom; Spain and Portugal were also kidnapping and enslaving people in Africa. The scholar Jason Idris Sparks goes further in his paper and draws an analogy between her and Elizabeth I: Elizabeth likewise employed the privateer Francis Drake and eventually knighted him. For these rulers and for the Barbarossa brothers, the motive was largely to defend Muslim territory and to strike back at the attacks on Muslims on the Iberian Peninsula.

points.h: She would not go to Fez, so the sultan came to marry her
points.body: In 1541 the sultan of Fez, Ahmad al-Wattasi, proposed marriage to her. By convention a sultan's bride would travel to Fez for the wedding and remain in the capital, but Sayyida al-Hurra refused to leave Tétouan; the sultan had to go to Tétouan himself for the wedding, and afterward she stayed on as ruler. As the show puts it, "this was not at all how it was usually done." The marriage was political, comparable to Ferdinand and Isabella uniting Aragon and Castile through marriage, and it established a link between the sultan and her family's Chefchaouen.

points.h: A coup by her son-in-law removed her, and the record nearly stops
points.body: Late in her rule, Ceuta cut off trade with Tétouan and the city's prosperity slipped somewhat. In 1542 her son-in-law Mulay Ahmed al-Hassan al-Mandri staged a coup and overthrew her; she lost her property and returned to Chefchaouen. The sources say very little about her life after that — only that she may have retired to a Sufi lodge, and that she died on 14 July 1561 with no children. The hosts note that later powerholders in Tétouan may have found her legacy threatening and been unwilling to acknowledge how a city prospered under a woman, which may be one reason the archive is so thin.

points.h: Europeans wrote her down, so she could only be a pirate
points.body: Most contemporary or near-contemporary accounts come from Europeans, which is why she is consistently written as a "pirate" rather than as a city-state leader or a sultana. Recent research is rewriting that frame: Jason Idris Sparks published a paper in the journal Religions in 2025 presenting her as an example of "early decolonial thought"; Amal Elhaimeur, who grew up in Morocco, has translated primary and secondary sources that previously had no English version. In 2016 a series about her also aired on Moroccan television.

quotes.text: A lot of European accounts of Sayda Alhurra's life characterize her as a pirate, and that is how we described her in that incredibly brief conversation in twenty sixteen that was mostly about not knowing anything

Sources are a little contradictory about exactly what Sayeda al Hua's relationship was with Oruche and Hazir. In some accounts she actively hired them as privateers, and others it was more like she allowed her own leaders and commanders to work with them, or she just tacitly allowed them to operate out of Tetuan.
But at this point, taking enemies prisoner and ransoming them back to their native countries was relatively common. A lot of countries were doing this long before they became famous as corsairs.

Beyond that, a big motivating factor for both Sayid al Hura and the Barbarossa Brothers was defending Muslim territory, including their own homes, against European incursions or retaliating against attacks on Muslims on the Iberian Peninsula during their lifetimes.
But Sayda al Hura refused to leave Tetuan. The Sultan traveled to her and after the wedding she stayed where she was and continued to rule Tetuan. This is not how it normally worked at all.

A lot of the contemporary or near contemporary mentions of her are from Europeans, which is also connected to why she is so often framed as a pirate, rather than as the leader of a city state or the queen of the sultanate.
